item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 7 of 7.

Tell Me Where It Hurts: The New Science of Pain and How to Heal – Rachel Zoffness Ph.D – (ebook)

This book appealed because both my wife and I are dealing with various and new forms of pain. We also expect that dealing with pain in one form or another will be a reasonably constant part of the rest of our lives.

Oh boy.

Traditional medicine deals with pain by applying medication. Unfortunately, that's generally not a successful long-term strategy. Zoffness invites us to examine the emotional, psychological, social, and environmental aspects of pain in addition to the physical. In doing so, we may find that there are additional strategies with a better long-term outlook.

Do this: Look beyond the purely physical.

item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 4 of 7.

Why Librarians Ask Before They Answer – Hana Lee Goldin, MLIS – (Card Catalog)

It's a lovely explainer, targeted at (what else) getting AI to act more like a librarian and ferret out what your question(s) really mean. It's a powerful technique and will almost certainly give you much better results than the typical "ask-answer-walk-away" approach we so often use with both search and AI.

> Search engines and chatbots answer what we give them directly, without asking what we meant. A chatbot can take the librarian's side of the interview, though, if we ask it to question us first.

Here's the thing: this is about so much more than search or AI. It's a mindset that, once adopted, lets you question yourself. Regardless of what tool you're using, or whether you're using any tool at all, the process of refining and clarifying just gets better answers.

The essay includes a prompt you can feed to your friendly neighborhood chatbot, of course, but structuring your own approach along the same lines is perhaps the most valuable takeaway of all.

Do this: Question yourself.

#ai #questions

item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 5 of 7.

If You're 21 And Terrified, Read This – JA Westenberg – (Blog)

Ignore the "21". This applies across the board at nearly any stage of life.

> Most of your choices are not final. People change jobs, cities, and social circles in their late twenties and thirties. You at twenty-one are not the same person you'll be at thirty. That's normal. It's not that you've messed up your twenties.

Again, ignore the twenty-one and thirty. Replace them with <your age> and <your age + 10>.

The advice Westenberg offers is ageless: become good at a skill; learn to sell; learn to write; build equity; learn to use AI tools; save and invest; take care of your health; don't date dickheads; be intentional with friendships; pick your location wisely; start asking for what you want; share your work; build a body of work; learn to recover quickly; take risks while you can; take back your attention; spend time with your parents; design your own life. None of those have expiration dates beyond our own.

As she points out: "Remember, you have both more and less time than you think."

Do this: Keep doing things.

#advice

item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 2 of 7.

A Short Guide To The Future – Mike Sowden – (Everything is Amazing)

In some ways, this last week has probably given many hope for more certainty in our future. It's also quite possible that things are just as uncertain as ever, just in different ways. While the only unchanging thing might be change itself, uncertainty is giving it a run for its money.

> Uncertainty is the heavy cloth of existence, and if you can learn to wear it without your knees buckling, it's oddly liberating.

Getting comfortable with uncertainty is a superpower, in my opinion. We can't know what happens next; what matters most is how we react to whatever comes.

Do this: Embrace more uncertainty.

item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 6 of 7.

Writing as a thinking tool – Murat – (Blog)

Another good overview of how writing is important when it comes to truly understanding something, though with a very heavy computer-science example to begin with. (You can ignore the example; I found it mildly interesting.)

This feels like the core argument that really speaks to me:

> When we write, we are externalizing our thinking onto paper, and that is what raises our capability to think bigger thoughts.

I see it as part of our evolution.

> Language let us externalize some of our thinking, and our species got smarter. Writing let us externalize even more of it, and we got smarter again.

Of course, much of this progress is threatened by AI, and the essay is a plea (and a how-to) to take that back.

Do this: Think bigger thoughts.

item.content:encoded:
From 7 Takeaways No. 301 — takeaway 3 of 7.

Ness Letters: The Comfort Paradox – Anne-Laure Le Cunff – (Ness Labs)

We live in amazing times. So much more is possible, and so much is being done for us; it's truly incredible. And yet almost everything we now see as "amazing" and "incredible" will someday, no doubt, be seen as normal and anything but noteworthy. And the results? The results will have less perceived value simply because they'll be considered mundane.

The argument here is that there's value in purposely adding difficulty to some of our tasks.

> We spend our lives trying to make everything easier, yet some of the things that make life worth living require difficulty.

I think the most obvious example right now might be how we connect with each other. It's trivial to message anyone anywhere on the planet and get a response in seconds. I won't say that this devalues the relationship, but it certainly makes it less "special" than a long-distance conversation might have been in the past. I'm also not saying that's an example of something we should purposely make more difficult. Far from it. But it is a tangible example of how ease can lead us to take for granted things that perhaps we should value more.

Do this: Consider whether some of the easy things in your life warrant a little more attention.
